question_text: Verify Rolle's theorem for the function f(x) = sin x − sin 2x on [0, π].

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Check the conditions on [0, π]
steps.margin_note: First mark. Both terms are 0 at each end. Write sin 2π = 0 explicitly — it is the value the examiner checks.
steps.memory_tip: Sine is 0 at every whole multiple of π, so sin π and sin 2π are both 0.
lines: (i) sin x and sin 2x are continuous for every real x, so f is continuous on [0, π]
(ii) sin x and sin 2x are differentiable for every real x, so f is differentiable on (0, π)
(iii) f(0) = sin 0 − sin 0 = 0 − 0 = 0  and  f(π) = sin π − sin 2π = 0 − 0 = 0
∴ f(0) = f(π) = 0, so Rolle's theorem applies on [0, π].

recall.must_convey: That sin x and sin 2x are continuous and differentiable everywhere, and that f(0) = f(π) = 0 because sin 0, sin π and sin 2π are all 0.
accept: sine functions are continuous and differentiable everywhere so the first two conditions hold

steps.why: For a trigonometric function the third condition is the one that can fail, so it is worth the full substitution. Both terms are 0 at x = 0 and again at x = π, which is what makes this interval the right one.
common_mistakes: Reading sin 2π as 2 sin π; sin 2π is the sine of the angle 2π, which is 0.
Excluding points from the domain, when sin x and sin 2x are defined and differentiable for every real x.

steps.label: Solve cos c − 2 cos 2c = 0
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Cos⁻¹ sends every value strictly between −1 and 1 to an angle strictly between 0 and π, so both roots give a usable c. Rolle's theorem requires only one such c; here there are two.
steps.memory_tip: A mixture of cos x and cos 2x becomes a quadratic only through cos 2x = 2cos²x − 1.
lines: √33 ≈ 5.745, so cos c ≈ 0.843 or cos c ≈ −0.593; both lie strictly between −1 and 1

lines.text: ∴ Rolle's theorem is verified, with c = Cos⁻¹((1 ± √33)/8), that is c ≈ 0.568 or c ≈ 2.206, both in (0, π)

recall.must_convey: That f′(x) = cos x − 2 cos 2x, that cos 2c = 2cos²c − 1 turns it into 4cos²c − cos c − 2 = 0, and that cos c = (1 ± √33)/8 gives c inside (0, π).
accept: differentiate to cos x minus two cos two x and use the double angle to get a quadratic in cos c

steps.why: The double angle has to be written in terms of cos c before the equation can be solved, because a mixture of cos c and cos 2c is not a quadratic. Of the three forms of cos 2c, only 2cos²c − 1 removes sin c and leaves a quadratic.
common_mistakes: Differentiating sin 2x as cos 2x and losing the factor 2.
Using cos 2c = 1 − 2sin²c, which leaves both sin c and cos c in the equation.
Discarding (1 − √33)/8 as impossible; it is about −0.593, which is a valid value of a cosine.
